analysis.topic_summary: This lesson teaches beginners how to define and call Python functions using the def keyword, and how to supply inputs to those functions. It covers the distinction between parameters (named placeholders in a function definition) and arguments (actual values passed when calling), as well as the two main ways to pass arguments: positional and keyword.

expected_facts: A function is defined in Python using the 'def' keyword followed by a function name, parentheses, and a colon
The code block inside a function must be indented consistently
A parameter is a named variable listed in the function definition's parentheses
An argument is the actual value passed to the function when it is called
Functions are called/invoked by writing the function name followed by parentheses containing any arguments
Positional arguments are matched to parameters based on their order in the call
Keyword arguments are passed as name=value pairs and matched by parameter name, not position
Keyword arguments can be passed in any order relative to each other
In a function call, positional arguments must appear before keyword arguments, or Python raises a SyntaxError
Parameters can have default values, defined with '=' in the function signature, making them optional when calling
A function without an explicit return statement returns None
The 'return' statement ends function execution and sends a value back to the caller
Calling a function with the wrong number of required positional arguments raises a TypeError
Variables created inside a function have local scope and are not accessible outside it
A docstring (triple-quoted string as the first statement in a function) documents what the function does

The statements that form the body of the function start at the next line, and

There are tools which use docstrings to automatically produce online or printed

referenced.

4.9.3.
Special parameters
¶

By default, arguments may be passed to a Python function either by position
or explicitly by keyword. For readability and performance, it makes sense to
restrict the way arguments can be passed so that a developer need only look
at the function definition to determine if items are passed by position, by
position or keyword, or by keyword.
A function definition may look like:
def f(pos1, pos2, /, pos_or_kwd, *, kwd1, kwd2):
 ----------- ---------- ----------
 | | |
 | Positional or keyword |
 | - Keyword only
 -- Positional only
where
/
and

*
are optional. If used, these symbols indicate the kind of
parameter by how the arguments may be passed to the function:
positional-only, positional-or-keyword, and keyword-only. Keyword parameters
are also referred to as named parameters.
4.9.3.1.
Positional-or-Keyword Arguments
¶
If
/
and
*
are not present in the function definition, arguments may
be passed to a function by position or by keyword.
4.9.3.2.
Positional-Only Parameters
¶

Looking at this in a bit more detail, it is possible to mark certain parameters
as
positional-only
. If
positional-only
, the parameters’ order matters, and
the parameters cannot be passed by keyword. Positional-only parameters are
placed before a
/
(forward-slash). The
/
is used to logically
separate the positional-only parameters from the rest of the parameters.
If there is no
/
in the function definition, there are no positional-only
parameters.
Parameters following the
/
may be
positional-or-keyword
or
keyword-only
.
4.9.3.3.
Keyword-Only Arguments
¶

Intermezzo: Coding Style
¶

4 spaces are a good compromise between small indentation (allows greater
nesting depth) and large indentation (easier to read). Tabs introduce
confusion, and are best left out.
Wrap lines so that they don’t exceed 79 characters.
This helps users with small displays and makes it possible to have several
code files side-by-side on larger displays.
Use blank lines to separate functions and classes, and larger blocks of
code inside functions.
When possible, put comments on a line of their own.
Use docstrings.
Use spaces around operators and after commas, but not directly inside
bracketing constructs:
a
=
f(1,
2)
+
g(3,
4)
.
Name your classes and functions consistently; the convention is to use

UpperCamelCase
for classes and
lowercase_with_underscores
for functions
and methods. Always use
self
as the name for the first method argument
(see
A First Look at Classes
for more on classes and methods).
Don’t use fancy encodings if your code is meant to be used in international
environments. Python’s default, UTF-8, or even plain ASCII work best in any
case.
Likewise, don’t use non-ASCII characters in identifiers if there is only the
slightest chance people speaking a different language will read or maintain
the code.

You might be thinking: "Wait a minute, I didn't see any return statement in the

(who):

'!'

)

(wd):

'ing'

(wd):

'ing'
)

print_ing(
'interest'

interesting

get_ing()

)

foo
'interesting'

'interest'

interesting
>>>
faa
>>>

len()

'eat'

>>>

# prints return value

'interest'

edit

In

for the definition of a function that returns a function, etc.

Function application

in these languages and in lambda calculus, so what looks like an application of a function to multiple arguments is correctly evaluated as the function applied to the first argument, then the resulting function applied to the second argument, etc.

An output argument must be an assignable variable, but it need not be initialized, any existing value is not accessible, and must be assigned a value. An input/output argument must be an initialized, assignable variable, and can optionally be assigned a value.

In some cases only input and input/output are distinguished, with output being considered a specific use of input/output, and in other cases only input and output (but not input/output) are supported. The default mode varies between languages: in Fortran 90 input/output is default, while in C# and SQL extensions input is default, and in TScript each parameter is explicitly specified as input or output.

Drawbacks
[
edit
]
Output parameters are often discouraged in modern programming, essentially as being awkward, confusing, and too low-level – commonplace return values are considerably easier to understand and work with.
[

Notably, output parameters involve functions with side effects (modifying the output parameter) and are semantically similar to references, which are more confusing than pure functions and values, and the distinction between output parameters and input/output parameters can be subtle. Further, since in common programming styles most parameters are simply input parameters, output parameters and input/output parameters are unusual and hence susceptible to misunderstanding.

content.title: Python Functions and Parameters
content.objective: Explain how to define and call Python functions, distinguish parameters from arguments, and demonstrate positional and keyword arguments.
content.overview: This lesson teaches you how to package reusable logic into Python functions using the `def` keyword, and how to supply data to those functions when you call them. You'll learn the precise difference between a parameter (the named slot in a function's definition) and an argument (the actual value you send in), and you'll practice both positional and keyword argument styles. By the end, you'll be able to write, call, and debug simple functions with confidence.
learning_objectives: Define a Python function using the `def` keyword, correct syntax, and consistent indentation
Call a Python function by name with the correct number of arguments, and explain what happens if you don't
Distinguish a parameter (defined in the function signature) from an argument (passed at call time)
Write and evaluate function calls that use positional arguments, where order determines matching
Write and evaluate function calls that use keyword arguments, including mixing positional and keyword correctly
content.audience: Beginner Python programmers who know basic syntax (variables, print, indentation) but have not yet written their own functions

sections.title: Why Functions Matter
sections.content:
### The problem functions solve
Imagine you need to greet 50 different users by name. Without functions, you'd copy-paste `print("Hello, " + name)` 50 times. A **function** lets you write that logic once and reuse it everywhere.

A Python function is a *self-contained block of code designed to perform a specific task*, which you can call and reuse in different parts of your program [S5]. Functions help organize code and make it more modular, reusable, and easier to maintain [S5].

### Analogy: a function is a vending machine
Think of a function like a vending machine. You don't need to know how it makes coffee internally — you just press a button (call it) and provide coins (arguments). It does its work and gives you a result (the return value). The machine's **slots** for coins are like **parameters**; the actual **coins you insert** are like **arguments**.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to build your own "vending machines" in Python.

sections.title: Before You Start
sections.content:
### You should already be comfortable with:
- Writing and running basic Python statements (e.g., `print()`, variable assignment)
- Python's use of **indentation** to define blocks (no curly braces) [S8]
- Basic data types: strings, integers, lists

### Tools needed
- Any Python 3 interpreter (python.org, an IDE, or an online REPL like the one at docs.python.org)

If you can run `print("hello")` and understand that indented lines belong to the same block as the `if` or `for` statement above them, you're ready.

sections.title: Defining and Calling Functions
sections.content:
### Defining a function
To write a Python function you need a **header** that starts with the `def` keyword, followed by the function name, an optional comma-separated list of parameters inside a required pair of parentheses, and a final colon [S8]. The function's **body** is indented one level to the right and holds the code that runs when the function is called [S8].

```python
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name)
```

Here, `def` is the keyword for defining a function; the function name (`greet`) is followed by parameter(s) in parentheses; the colon signals the start of the function body, marked by indentation [S4].

### Calling a function
You **call** a function by writing its name followed by parentheses, which enclose any necessary arguments [S5]:

```python
greet("Maria")   # Output: Hello, Maria
```

The parentheses are *always required* in a call — even with zero arguments — because leaving them off just references the function object instead of running it [S8].

### Parameters vs. arguments
This is a precise but often-confused pair of terms:

| Term | Where it lives | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| **Parameter** | Function *definition* | The named variable listed inside the parentheses when the function is defined [S2] |
| **Argument** | Function *call* | The actual value sent to the function when it is called [S10] |

```python
def greet(name):      # 'name' is a PARAMETER
    print("Hello, " + name)

greet("Maria")         # "Maria" is an ARGUMENT
```

From the function's perspective: the parameter is the placeholder; the argument is what fills it in at run time [S6]. The two terms are often used loosely as synonyms, but being precise helps you read error messages correctly.

### Matching counts: required arguments
By default, a function must be called with the exact number of arguments it expects [S10]. Calling `greet()` with zero arguments when `greet` requires one raises:

```
TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'
```

Calling `greet("A", "B")` with two arguments when `greet` only accepts one raises a different `TypeError`, because Python distinguishes missing arguments from extra arguments [S5][S7]:

```
TypeError: greet() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
```

### Positional arguments
**Positional arguments** are matched to parameters strictly by their order in the call [S9][S5]. The first argument fills the first parameter, the second fills the second, and so on.

```python
def describe_pet(animal, name):
    print(f"{name} is a {animal}")

describe_pet("dog", "Rex")   # animal='dog', name='Rex'
describe_pet("Rex", "dog")   # Swapped! animal='Rex', name='dog' — likely wrong
```

### Keyword arguments
**Keyword arguments** are passed as `name=value` pairs and are matched by parameter name rather than position [S7][S2]. This removes the ordering restriction entirely — if you use keyword arguments, order does not matter [S9][S5]:

```python
describe_pet(animal="dog", name="Rex")
describe_pet(name="Rex", animal="dog")   # Same result, different order
```

### The ordering rule: positional before keyword
In a single call you *can* mix positional and keyword arguments, but **positional arguments must come before keyword arguments**, or Python raises a `SyntaxError` [S9][S7]:

```python
describe_pet("dog", name="Rex")   # OK: positional first, then keyword
describe_pet(animal="dog", "Rex")  # SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument
```

### Default parameter values
You can give a parameter a **default value** using `=` in the function signature, which makes that argument optional when calling [S9]:

```python
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}")

greet("Sam")                 # Hello, Sam  (default used)
greet("Sam", "Hi")           # Hi, Sam     (default overridden)
```

Non-default parameters must come before default parameters in the definition; placing a default parameter first causes a `SyntaxError` [S9][S7].

### Return values
The `return` statement ends function execution and sends a value back to the caller [S1][S8]. If no `return` statement is present, Python implicitly returns `None` [S8].

```python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(2, 3)   # result = 5
```

### Function (local) scope
Variables created inside a function exist only in that function's **local scope** and are not accessible from outside it [S1]. Each call creates a fresh local symbol table [S1].

### Docstrings
A **docstring** — a triple-quoted string as the very first statement in a function body — documents what the function does:

```python
def add(a, b):
    """Return the sum of a and b."""
    return a + b
```

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
### Example 1 — Define, call, and trace execution
```python
def f(x):
    return x**2 + 1

print(f(4))   # 17
```
Step by step: `def f(x):` defines function `f` with parameter `x`. Calling `f(4)` passes argument `4`, binding `x = 4` inside the function. The body computes `4**2 + 1 = 17` and `return` sends `17` back to the caller [S4].

### Example 2 — Positional order matters
```python
def student(fn, ln='Mark', std='Fifth'):
    print(fn, ln, 'studies in', std, 'Standard')

student('John')                  # John Mark studies in Fifth Standard
student('John', 'Gates', 'Seventh')  # John Gates studies in Seventh Standard
student('John', 'Gates')         # John Gates studies in Fifth Standard
```
Notice how positional arguments fill in left to right, and any parameter not supplied falls back to its default [S9].

### Example 3 — Keyword arguments in any order
```python
def calculate_cost(item, quantity, price):
    print(f"{quantity} {item} cost ${quantity * price:.2f}")

calculate_cost(price=0.74, quantity=6, item="bananas")
# 6 bananas cost $4.44
```
Because each argument is named, Python unambiguously matches it to the correct parameter regardless of order [S5].

### Example 4 — Common errors
```python
def add_item(item_name, quantity):
    print(f"{quantity}x {item_name}")

add_item()
# TypeError: add_item() missing 2 required positional arguments: 'item_name' and 'quantity'

add_item(item_name="Bread", "3")
# SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument
```
The first error occurs because required arguments were omitted [S7]; the second because a positional argument was placed after a keyword argument [S9].

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
- **Data validation functions**: `def is_valid_email(address):` — called with one positional argument wherever you need to check input.
- **Configurable reports**: `def generate_report(data, title="Report", include_chart=False):` — keyword arguments let callers customize only the options they care about, leaving sensible defaults for the rest [S7].
- **APIs and libraries**: Many Python library functions (e.g., `print(*objects, sep=' ', end='\n')`) rely on keyword arguments so users don't have to memorize argument order for rarely-used options.

sections.title: Practical Activity: Build and Call Your Own Function
sections.content:
### Task
1. Open a Python interpreter or file.
2. Define a function `book_ticket` with three parameters: `name`, `destination`, and `seat="Economy"` (default value).
   ```python
   def book_ticket(name, destination, seat="Economy"):
       """Print a booking confirmation."""
       print(f"{name} is booked to {destination} in {seat} class.")
   ```
3. Call the function **three** different ways (one call per line, so you can compare outputs):
   - Using only positional arguments, including `seat`.
   - Using keyword arguments in a different order than the parameter list.
   - Mixing positional and keyword correctly (positional first), omitting `seat` so the default is used.
4. Deliberately write one call that puts a keyword argument before a positional one, run it, and read the error message.

### Expected outcome
- Calls 1–3 print correct booking confirmations; call 2 shows the default `seat` value overridden.
- Call 4 raises `SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument` — confirming the ordering rule [S9].

### Self-check
- Can you explain, in your own words, why call 4 failed?
- Can you identify which lines are parameters and which are arguments in your code?

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
- Define functions with `def name(parameters):` followed by an indented body [S8].
- Call functions with `name(arguments)`; parentheses are always required [S8].
- **Parameters** live in the definition; **arguments** are the values passed at call time [S2][S10].
- **Positional arguments** match by order; **keyword arguments** match by name and can appear in any order relative to each other [S9][S5].
- Positional arguments must come before keyword arguments in a call, or you get a `SyntaxError` [S9].
- Default values (`param=value`) make arguments optional [S9]; missing required arguments raise `TypeError` [S7].
- `return` sends a value back to the caller; without it, a function returns `None` [S8].
- Variables defined inside a function are local to that function [S1].

Its main weakness is pacing: the concepts section folds in several non-objective topics (return, scope, docstrings) that crowd out time for the core positional/keyword material, and both the activity and knowledge check pack more cognitive work than their minute allotments realistically support, with the activity's final step also risking a confusing script-wide failure for beginners.
qc_instructional.methodology: Score = sum of ten rubric criteria scored 0-10 by an independent instructional-design review: Learning objective alignment, Explanation clarity, Logical sequence, Concept completeness, Quality of examples, Practical applicability, Student engagement, Knowledge-check relevance, Difficulty progression, 45-minute time compliance. The time-compliance criterion is forced to 0 by code when section minutes exceed 45. Deterministic checks add issues for missing required sections, fewer than 4 knowledge checks, or objective parts with no knowledge check. Verdict: 'Needs revision' if any critical issue, any objective part not covered, the 45-minute limit is exceeded, or score < 70; 'Passed' if score >= 85 and no high-severity issue; otherwise 'Passed with recommendations'.

rubric.note: All five objective parts (def keyword, calling, parameter/argument distinction, positional args, keyword args) are explicitly taught in the concepts section, reinforced in worked examples, practiced in the activity, and directly tested in the knowledge check. Alignment is tight and traceable end-to-end.

The vending-machine analogy, the parameter-vs-argument comparison table, and the explicit TypeError/SyntaxError examples are unusually clear for a beginner audience. One clarity gap: the lesson never explains that a SyntaxError is a parse-time failure (before any code runs) while a TypeError is a run-time failure, which matters for how the activity's error-producing call behaves relative to the other calls.

Def → call → parameter/argument distinction → required-argument errors → positional → keyword → ordering rule → defaults → return → scope → docstrings is a sensible progression for the core objective, but return/scope/docstrings are inserted as if core material even though they sit outside the stated objective, adding length without a matching time allowance.

Every objective part is covered in depth, and the lesson even goes beyond it (defaults, return values, scope, docstrings), which is generous for completeness but creates downstream timing pressure (see timing criterion).

Four worked examples progress from a simple trace, to positional defaults, to pure keyword matching, to two distinct error types — strong variety and realistic patterns (student records, cost calculator). The error-timing nuance between the TypeError and SyntaxError examples in Example 4 is not explained, which is a minor clarity gap for examples otherwise well-chosen.

Real-World Applications gives plausible use cases (validation, configurable reports, print()'s signature) but stays at the bullet-point level with no runnable code, so at only 2 minutes it reads more like a list than an application. The activity itself (ticket booking) is a good practical scenario.

The 13-minute concepts section is a long, dense run of prose + code blocks with no embedded checkpoint or 'predict the output' prompt until the learner reaches the separate Examples section; engagement relies almost entirely on the activity and knowledge check to break up passive reading.

Each question maps to a distinct objective part (Q1 def, Q2 call semantics, Q3 parameter/argument, Q4 positional, Q5 keyword, Q6 ordering rule). Q5's distractors are especially strong (D tests a subtle 'multiple values for argument' case). Mixing 3 open-response and 3 MC items is pedagogically fine but adds time risk (see timing).

Progression from single-parameter greet() to multi-parameter describe_pet() to defaults in student() to all-keyword calculate_cost() to intentional error cases is well-graded; the activity mirrors this by building up to a deliberately broken call.

Arithmetic sums to 45, but per-section load is unrealistic for true beginners: 13 minutes for ~11 subtopics (def, call, params vs args, required-argument errors, positional, keyword, ordering, defaults, return, scope, docstrings) is dense reading alone, let alone comprehension; the 7-minute activity asks a beginner to write a function, make 4 calls, run two different error types, and self-reflect; the 6-minute knowledge check mixes 3 constructed-response items with 3 MC items. Each of these three sections likely needs materially more time than allotted, or the extraneous content (return/scope/docstrings) needs to be trimmed to make room.

issues.original_text:
### Return values
The `return` statement ends function execution and sends a value back to the caller [S1][S8]. If no `return` statement is present, Python implicitly returns `None` [S8].

```python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(2, 3)   # result = 5
```

### Function (local) scope
Variables created inside a function exist only in that function's **local scope** and are not accessible from outside it [S1]. Each call creates a fresh local symbol table [S1].

### Docstrings
A **docstring** — a triple-quoted string as the very first statement in a function body — documents what the function does:

```python
def add(a, b):
    """Return the sum of a and b."""
    return a + b
```
issues.suggested_text:
### Beyond this lesson
Two quick facts for later: a function can send a value back to its caller with `return` (and returns `None` automatically if you never use `return`), and variables created inside a function only exist inside that function (its **local scope**) — they're not visible outside it. You can also document a function with a **docstring**, a triple-quoted string right after `def`:

```python
def add(a, b):
    """Return the sum of a and b."""
    return a + b
```

We'll dig into `return` and scope properly in a later lesson — for now, keep your focus on defining, calling, and passing positional/keyword arguments.

issues.problem: Step 4 tells the learner to write the keyword-before-positional call as another line in the same file as calls 1–3, then 'run it.' In Python, a SyntaxError is raised when the file is parsed, before any line executes — so if call 4 stays in the same file, calls 1–3 will never print anything either, contradicting the stated expected outcome.
issues.why: A beginner running the whole file and seeing no output at all (not even the first three correct confirmations) will likely be confused about why 'nothing worked,' undermining the very outcome the activity is trying to produce.
issues.original_text: 4. Deliberately write one call that puts a keyword argument before a positional one, run it, and read the error message.
issues.suggested_text: 4. First run the file with only calls 1–3 and confirm all three booking confirmations print correctly. Then, on a new line below them, add a call that puts a keyword argument before a positional one (e.g., `book_ticket(name="Ana", "Paris")`), save, and run the file again just to see the error message — then comment that line back out before moving on.

issues.problem: The expected-outcome bullets state calls 1–3 print correctly and call 4 raises a SyntaxError, but don't clarify that a SyntaxError anywhere in a Python file blocks the entire file from running — so if call 4 is left in place alongside calls 1–3, the learner would see only the error and no prints at all, not both outcomes simultaneously.
issues.why: Without this clarification, learners may think they did something wrong when calls 1–3 don't print once call 4 is added, rather than understanding this as expected Python behavior.
issues.original_text: - Call 4 raises `SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument` — confirming the ordering rule [S9].
issues.suggested_text: - Call 4 raises `SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument` — confirming the ordering rule [S9]. Because Python detects this error while reading the file, before running anything, test call 4 by itself (temporarily removing or commenting out calls 1–3, or adding call 4 only after you've already seen calls 1–3 succeed) rather than expecting both outcomes from a single run.

issues.problem: The explanation names why each error occurs but never distinguishes that the TypeError happens at call/run time while the SyntaxError happens at parse time (before the program runs at all), even though both are presented back-to-back as if encountered the same way.
issues.why: Without this distinction, learners can't correctly predict what happens when a SyntaxError-causing line sits in a larger script (e.g., in the Practical Activity), and may misunderstand Python's error model more broadly.
issues.original_text: The first error occurs because required arguments were omitted [S7]; the second because a positional argument was placed after a keyword argument [S9].
issues.suggested_text: The first error occurs because required arguments were omitted [S7] — this is a `TypeError`, detected when Python actually tries to run the call. The second occurs because a positional argument was placed after a keyword argument [S9] — this is a `SyntaxError`, detected while Python reads the file, *before* any code runs. That means a single bad `SyntaxError` line can stop an entire script from running at all, not just the one call.

issues.problem: Six minutes is allotted for 6 questions, but 3 of them (Q1, Q3, Q6) are open constructed-response items requiring the learner to compose a written explanation, not just select an answer — this takes meaningfully longer per item than a multiple-choice question.
issues.why: At a true 1-minute-per-question pace, learners won't have time to actually think through and write out explanations for the open-response items, turning the check into a skim-the-answer exercise rather than genuine retrieval practice.
